vignette:
She sits at her sewing machine, the needle punching through fabric in a rhythm she has known since she was twelve. The shop is small, tucked behind a row of spice stalls, and the air smells of turmeric and jute. She keeps her back to the door. Her husband, Ravi, brings her tea in the mornings, and she thanks him without lifting her eyes. They have been married for four years—long enough for the neighbors to stop asking why she never goes to the market alone.

It began in the second year of the marriage. Her in-laws, displeased with her dowry, found fault in everything—the way she folded the bedsheets, the salt in the dal. Her husband, at first, defended her. Then he stopped. One evening he came home with red eyes and a leather belt. She remembers the buckle, cold against her spine. He told her she was ungrateful, that her family had shamed him. She believed him. Over the next eighteen months, the belt became a cord, the cord became an iron rod, the rod became a sliver of glass held to her throat while he whispered that no one would hear her scream through the plaster walls.

She stopped eating with the family. She stopped sleeping in their bed. She spent hours at the sewing machine, fingers moving by rote, because the whir of the motor drowned out the sound of his footsteps. But the design of a *salwar kameez* requires precision—a straight seam at the neckline, a clean hem. She began making mistakes. She would measure twice, cut once, and still the sleeve would come out twisted. Her hands would shake, and she would see, in the grain of the cotton, the pattern of the rope marks on her wrists.

She left him twice. The first time, she walked to her mother’s house, three towns over. Her mother cried and told her that a wife’s duty was to endure. She sent her back the next morning with a bag of mangoes. The second time, she called the police. A constable came, looked at the bruises on her ribs, and said it was a domestic matter. She returned to the tailor shop because she didn’t know where else to go. She had no money of her own—the shop belongs to Ravi’s uncle. Every stitch she sews in his name.

Now she is twenty-eight, and the torture has stopped. Not because he is sorry, but because she stopped crying, stopped resisting, became a piece of furniture. He calls her his good wife. She feels nothing when he touches her. But at night, she dreams of the glass against her throat, and she wakes with her hand clamped over her mouth, stifling a scream. She cannot stand the smell of leather. The sight of a coiled belt on a chair makes her sweat. She wears only *dupattas* that cover her collarbone, even in summer.

Her customers compliment her work, but she no longer believes them. She hears their words as veiled threats. When a woman asks for a tighter neckline, she thinks the woman wants to strangle her. She counts the minutes until the shop closes. She counts the stitches in a seam. If she stops counting, her mind fills with red.

Yesterday, on the street, a man dropped a metal spoon. The clatter sent her to the ground, hands over her head, gasping. Ravi’s uncle said she was possessed. She didn’t correct him. She can’t explain that the sound is his footsteps. The sound is the rod hitting the floor. The sound is her own teeth shattering.

She drinks chai now only in small sips, watching the steam rise, because once, in the long terror, he held her head underwater in the bathtub. She cannot bathe without leaving the door open. She does not own a mirror. Her hair has grown long and tangled because she cannot bear to look at her own face—she sees his reflection in her eyes.

She still goes to the shop. She still sews. Her hands remember a life before the pain, but her body remembers only the pain. When the needle jams, she flinches. When a customer laughs, she startles. She lives waiting for the next blow, even though no blow comes. The torture has ended, but the fear has not. It lives in the whip-lash of each thread.
